props.title: The Soft Skin
props.initialSlug: Married professor's passionate affair leads to tragedy

sections.content: François Truffaut's The Soft Skin (1964) marks a fascinating departure from his earlier New Wave works, trading youthful exuberance for a mature exploration of infidelity. Unlike the playful energy of Jules and Jim (1962), Truffaut crafts a taut psychological drama that owes more to Hitchcock's influence than the freewheeling spirit of the French New Wave. The film follows Pierre, a married literary scholar who begins an affair with a flight attendant, Nicole. Truffaut's camera work is methodical and precise, building tension through careful framing and extended sequences that heighten the protagonist's moral descent.

sections.content: The influence of The Soft Skin reverberates through later French cinema's treatment of infidelity and bourgeois marriage. Claude Chabrol's La Femme Infidèle (1969) echoes its clinical examination of adultery, while Maurice Pialat's We Won't Grow Old Together (1972) shares its unflinching look at relationship dysfunction. Truffaut's film pioneered a more sophisticated approach to depicting marital discord, moving beyond simple moral judgments to explore the psychological complexity of betrayal.

Technically, The Soft Skin demonstrates Truffaut's evolution as a filmmaker. The director employs techniques learned from his extensive interviews with Alfred Hitchcock, published later in Hitchcock/Truffaut (1966). The airport sequences, in particular, showcase masterful suspense building that would influence later French thrillers like The Butcher (1970) and Henri-Georges Clouzot's final film La Prisonnière (1968). movies.title: La Peau Douce
movies.slug: Original French title of The Soft Skin, essential for understanding Truffaut's filmography

sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing inspiration from The Soft Skin's (1964) sophisticated approach to adultery. Olivier Assayas's Double Lives (2018) and Mia Hansen-Løve's Things to Come (2016) echo its exploration of intellectual life intersecting with emotional crisis. The film's influence extends beyond French cinema, visible in works like Todd Field's Little Children (2006) and Richard Linklater's Before Midnight (2013), which share its nuanced approach to marriage and infidelity.
